summary: The video teaches an intraday options day-trading routine limited to the first ~90 minutes of the session. It defines a 'No Trading Zone' from the pre-market high/low and yesterday's high/low, and uses a 200 SMA on 2-, 5- and 10-minute charts as the direction filter (calls above, puts below). Entries come on the candle after a retest of a broken 15-minute opening range. Exits are scale-outs at hand-drawn hourly support/resistance levels, and position size grows after the first trade ('bell curve' sizing). The video ends with a pitch for a paid mentorship.
why_not_testable: The real strategy runs on intraday bars (2-, 5- and 10-minute charts, a 15-minute opening range, pre-market high/low). The daily-bar backtester cannot represent it; only a rough daily proxy is possible.
Half the trades are puts, i.e. short exposure. The long-only backtester can only test the bullish (calls) side.
Profit targets come from discretionary hand-drawn levels at 'every bend' on an hourly line chart. Extra confluence (Fibonacci 0.236/0.382, 8 EMA, news checks) is applied by judgment.

strategies.name: NTZ Breakout + 200 SMA Trend (daily proxy of ORB/NTZ day-trade, long side)
strategies.description: Rough daily-bar approximation of the speaker's intraday system. Go long only when price is above the 200 SMA (the 'truth filter') and has broken out above yesterday's high (the top of the 'No Trading Zone'). Hold for at most one day, because the original is an intraday trade. This does NOT capture the 15-minute opening range, the retest-then-next-candle entry, pre-market levels or hand-drawn profit levels.
missing: Uses intraday bars: 2-min (first 30 min), 5-min (10:00-11:00), 10-min (after 11:00). The 200 SMA is computed on those charts, not on daily bars.
Entry trigger is a break of the first 15-minute opening range (9:30-9:45), then a retest, with entry on the candle AFTER the retest. This is not expressible on daily bars.
The NTZ uses the pre-market high/low (extended hours) as well as yesterday's high/low. Pre-market data is not available in daily bars.
Stop loss is 'on the other side of the ORB' or the other side of a Fibonacci level. No fixed percentage is given.
Profit targets are hand-drawn hourly levels, with partial scale-outs at each level and runners held on trend days. No fixed percentage is given.
Short side: puts are bought when price is below the 200 SMA. Shorting is not supported by the long-only backtester.
Trading window is restricted to roughly the first 90 minutes of the session.
Bell-curve position sizing: small first trade, size up when in rhythm, size down or stop when red.
assumptions: Used the 200-day SMA as a stand-in for the 200 SMA on intraday charts.
Used close above the previous day's high (highest, period 1) as a proxy for 'fully breaking out of the NTZ' to the upside. Pre-market high is ignored.
Set max_hold_days=1 to reflect that this is a day trade.
Set a 1% stop as a conservative placeholder for 'other side of the ORB'.
Added an exit on close crossing below the 200 SMA, as a stand-in for the trend filter flipping.
Symbol SPY is a default; the video does not name the ticker traded.

evidence.quote: And then I use my truth filter, 200 simple moving average. If the price is above the 200 simple moving average, I'm thinking calls. Below the 200 simple moving average, I'm thinking puts.
NTZ is built using pre-market high, pre-market low, yesterday's high, and yesterday's low.
the only time we can actually enter into the trade is once we fully completely break out of this range.
Opening range breakout is the range of first 15 minutes into the market open... I don't chase breakouts. I wait for the retest, break, pull back, structure, entry.
We do not enter on the retest candle. We entered on the next candle of the retest.
Stop loss is on the other side of the ORB.
So these levels simply become my profit taking areas. When price hits a level, I'm scaling out of a position.
In my experience, you do not need more than 90 minutes to day trade.
First 30 minutes of the day after the market open, I'm on a two-minute chart. From 10:00 to 11:00, I'm on a 5 minute chart. And after 11:00, that's when I switch to 10-minute chart.
First trade of the day is always going to be with a small position size. If the market is clean, I'm in the rhythm, I'll size up.

non_mechanical_ideas: Draw levels at 'every bend' on an hourly line chart with extended hours, two or three above and below price, then nudge them to touch wicks on candlesticks. Levels are used for exits, not entries.
Inside the NTZ, take no trades, or only very small size if a setup is exceptionally clean.
Wait for the first 15 minutes before trading; the speaker occasionally makes exceptions based on structure.
Check the economic calendar (Fed speakers, 10:00/10:30 releases) and be extra careful around news.
Seek confluence before entering: Fibonacci pullback to 0.236/0.382 on strong days, a bounce off the 8 EMA, or a retest of the ORB/pre-market high or hourly levels.
Let runners run on clean trend days instead of panic-taking profits.
Backtest using TradingView bar replay at random dates with the chart hidden to avoid bias; journal every trade.
Psychology: patience, cash is a position, avoid overtrading and revenge trading, stop trading when red or unsure.
The end of the video is a sales pitch for a paid live trading room and mentorship.
options_notes: The speaker trades options intraday: buys calls when price is above the 200 SMA and puts when below, triggered by the ORB/NTZ break-and-retest. No strikes, deltas or expirations are given (likely short-dated, day-trade holds). Positions are scaled out at hand-drawn levels, e.g. '10 contracts... taken five off' at the first level and more at the next. Size is added on later retests (e.g. of the 200/400 SMA or the NTZ edge), using 'bell curve' sizing that starts small on the first trade.
